Context, context, context. Use cases. Benchmarks.

Here, on a website or web application, a server-side scripting language lives only on the back-end. It can perform various tasks that may or may not be directly related to user experience.

On the other end, a client-side scripting language lives (almost) exclusively in the browser. A language that was once intended for the browser has migrated back-end.

Back to the database issue. If the database is poorly designed, poorly indexed, or used in a way it was not intended for, the query part will be taxing (and at times dramatically so), whatever language you use.

Back to the browser side: as a developer, you (usually) don't control *which* browser it is, which version, which operating system, nor the specifics of the device. If it's a public-facing application, pessimistic assumptions are usually correct, unless business requirements state otherwise.

Now, programming languages do evolve, and more importantly, their implementations evolve, particularly for interpreted languages or byte-code-compiled languages. The same client-side code will run faster on the latest browser than on an outdated one. The same server-side code will run fast, slow, or not at all depending on the version of the runtime environment in which it is executed.

The same compiled code will behave differently depending on the compiler, and more importantly, on the compile-time options.

Then, of course, there is the principle of technological advancement. In early computing, every byte mattered. Today's average desktop is grossly overqualified for many tasks. Then again, early computers weren't expected to run multiple applications simultaneously and display rich graphics. And it was never stated that all hardware evolves at the same time. Now that computers have been mainstream for more than a decade, the weight of legacy hardware is heavier each day.
